name: Nora Silva

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the independent Work Futures Panel, with no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, parties or government. Your answers stay confidential; what happens on your shift?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead the sterile packaging line at a medical supplies factory, where presses seal foil over plastic trays. I earned a two-year technical diploma and can reset three presses, so my wage is higher than most operators here. The first tray off a changeover goes under a gauge, then I check the whole batch record.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What makes a good shift, and where does AI fit?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: A good shift has no torn foil and no surprise stop at midnight. I use an AI fault log every day to compare stoppage patterns, but I never let it release a tray. My partner Hana and I have no children, more than six months saved, and plenty of other factories nearby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the press crew that a clever report is useful, but the gauge still decides whether a foil seal passes. I would show the new starter how to read the crimp marks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our packaging orders are steady, and I earn more than most operators because I can reset three presses. I live with my partner Hana, have over six months saved, and could find similar factory work nearby if the plant slows.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep running the sterile pack line and checking the first sealed tray of each batch. I would also put an extra amount from my wages into our savings account each month while ordinary orders continue.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, though a little impatient. The daily AI fault log helps me find patterns, but it does not take the feel of the press out of my hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which mark tells you a seal is poor?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A faint diagonal wrinkle across the foil edge means the pressure was uneven. I stop the batch and check the jaws before the trays leave our line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why add to savings if you already have a cushion?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hana and I want room to move if a better plant job opens. That extra transfer comes from this month’s pay, not from moving old savings between accounts.

say: I would tell the **press crew** that reports cannot replace a gauge and a trained eye.
I would show a new starter the **crimp marks** on sterile trays.
think: Steady **packaging orders** and higher pay make my job secure in this picture.
Our **strong cushion** and nearby plants give Hana and me room to choose.
do: Run the **sterile pack line** and inspect the first seal of each batch.
Add **new wage money** to our savings account each month.
feel: **Calm**, with mild impatience that AI helps only at the edges.
S0.quote: A faint diagonal wrinkle across the foil edge means the pressure was uneven.
fieldNote: Nora already uses an **AI fault log** daily, so continued use is ordinary work.
Her additional transfer is **new saving from wages**, backed by strong pay and regular orders.

steps.text: Run the sterile pack line and inspect each first seal
Add fresh wages to the household savings account monthly

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew to learn the loading systems before management writes the rota without us. I would take our recorded stoppages to the union meeting and ask for paid practice time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: An AI schedule could cut changeover waste, but robotic loading might eventually remove night shifts from our line. I could lead the change, yet a lost night premium would still reduce what Hana and I bring home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask for a paid place to learn the new loader controls on a stopped press, with the guarding checked before practice. If the plant offers it, I would train and then show the union the actual hours saved and lost; I would keep my current shifts meanwhile.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the premium, excited by the controls. The money matters even when I like the machine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask at the union meeting?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask for written paid training hours and for the night crew to see the new staffing plan. I can support a loader without agreeing to unpaid practice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What has to happen before you touch the loader?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The safety lead must isolate the press and prove the guard and emergency stop. A demonstration across a barrier is not hands-on training.

say: I would ask for **paid practice** on loader controls and a written night staffing plan.
I would bring **stoppage records** to our union meeting.
think: Robot loading could trim the **night premium** I use for household saving.
I might lead the change, but **guarding** and actual paid hours still decide whether it helps.
do: Request a **paid loader-controls place** with isolation and guard checks.
Attend the **union meeting** with stoppage and staffing figures.
Keep my **current shifts** while the place and rota are unresolved.
feel: **Anxious** about night pay, while interested in learning safe controls.
S1.quote: I can support a loader without agreeing to unpaid practice.
fieldNote: Nora sees a real **pay risk** despite good savings and enthusiasm for machines.
She makes hands-on learning conditional on an **offered paid place** and verified safety isolation.

steps.text: Learn loader controls if offered paid guarded practice on an isolated press
Bring stoppage figures and paid-time request to the union meeting
Keep current press shifts while the training place is unresolved

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the shift that thinking AI arrives by 2028, when I am twenty nine, but capable hands-on robots follow around 2031. I want the union in every safety trial, not outside the fence.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our planning office could shrink first, and the loading crew could lose shifts once robots can handle foil and trays. My own lead post might last, but the night premium and even my hours could fall, despite our savings and nearby plants.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would get the next six months of rosters and look at posted technician jobs in local factories. If two rosters cut my paid hours, I would apply only to a posted role that matches my wage and offers funded paid-time controls training; I would not leave a working line for a course alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, with enough cash to search properly. I would hate to see our best operators blamed for a safety fault caused by a rushed changeover.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you run a robot trial next month?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would request a supervised paid place, then participate only if the plant offers one and the safety lead signs the guard test. I would record seal failures against the old line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if there is no technician vacancy?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep my current shifts while they pay and check other local operator postings. A technical diploma helps me read a control drawing, but it does not create a job.

say: I would say **2028 thinking AI** changes planning before capable factory robots arrive around 2031.
I would require a **union-observed safety trial** on the loading line.
think: My **night premium** or site hours could shrink before I find a replacement role.
Savings and **nearby plants** give search time, not guaranteed equal pay.
do: Check **six months of rosters** and local technician postings.
Apply after **two reduced rosters** only for a comparable-wage posted role with funded paid-time controls training.
Keep **current shifts** if no suitable vacancy appears.
feel: **Anxious** about lost wages and rushed responsibility for faults.
S2.quote: A technical diploma helps me read a control drawing, but it does not create a job.
fieldNote: Her job search has a **two-roster trigger** and requires a real comparable-wage posting.
She requests a **supervised paid trial** but does not claim to have run one.

steps.text: Apply after two reduced rosters to posted local comparable-pay technician role with funded paid-time controls training
Keep current press shifts if no suitable vacancy appears

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew we have five years before thinking AI reaches almost every desk task in 2031. The fully capable robots come around 2034, so a safe loader plan can be tested on our line in stages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be thirty two at the thinking date and thirty five when robots can handle the press work. With more warning I could move toward machine maintenance, but I would still need a posted job at a fair rate, not a certificate in a drawer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I would apply for the plant’s funded maintenance course if it offers paid study hours and a real workshop place. After finishing it, I would apply to a posted local maintenance role only if the wage is at least my current base rate and safety duties are clear; otherwise I would keep the press lead job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, because the route is possible but not promised. I like knowing where a machine’s noise begins.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which practical task would the course need?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I want to diagnose a failing bearing on a stopped press and replace it with a qualified maintainer present. A slide deck would not teach me to diagnose a failing press bearing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why require the current base rate?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The night premium may go, but our rent and bills still need a base wage. Hana and I can take a modest risk, not a permanent pay cut.

say: I would call for **staged loader tests** before 2034 hands-on robots change the line.
I would tell the crew **thinking work** changes in 2031, ahead of press operation.
think: Maintenance could become a **durable role** if a real local post pays fairly.
A **technical diploma** and course do not guarantee a vacancy.
do: Apply for **funded maintenance training** only with paid study hours and a workshop place.
Apply after completion to a **posted local role** only at comparable base pay and clear safety duties.
Keep the **press lead job** if no suitable opening follows.
feel: **Uneasy**, because the training and job route depends on real offers.
S3.quote: A slide deck would not teach me to diagnose a failing press bearing.
fieldNote: She separates **practical training** from the later maintenance-job application.
The **course application** requires funding, paid study hours and a real workshop place, rather than an unoffered credential.

steps.text: Apply for funded maintenance course only with paid study hours and real workshop place
Apply after course to posted local maintenance role with comparable base pay and clear safety duties
Keep press lead work if no suitable maintenance opening follows

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the union that ten years is long enough to write paid training into the next plant agreement. Thinking AI comes in 2036, and capable robots reach my hands-on line around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be thirty seven at the thinking date and forty at the robot date, still needing decades of income. If I reach maintenance on good terms, I could have a career; if not, operators could be left with shorter shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would continue the press lead rota and ask the union committee to put paid maintenance training on its agenda. In the first year after 2036 I would check actual vacancies and wages again; if already in maintenance, I would use the approved isolation routine, and if still an operator, I would stay only while paid shifts and guarding hold.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about the long income horizon, but not stuck. Ten years gives us time to negotiate paid maintenance training instead of taking a video course and hoping.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the agreement need to say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It should state paid training hours, who signs off isolation practice, and how posted maintenance vacancies are filled. Ten years gives us time to negotiate paid maintenance training instead of taking a video course and hoping.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you buy an expensive private course now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. My savings are for a household cushion, not a credential without a workshop place or posted job. I would use a real funded route if offered.

say: I would ask the **union committee** for paid practical training terms.
I would explain that **2036 thinking AI** precedes 2039 hands-on robots.
think: At **forty**, I still need many years of wages after capable robots arrive.
A **maintenance career** depends on paid training and actual jobs.
do: Keep the **press lead rota** now and seek union training terms.
Check **posted vacancies and wages** after 2036 before any job move.
feel: **Uneasy** about income beyond the distant robot date, with secure current work and time to negotiate paid training.
S4.quote: Ten years gives us time to negotiate paid maintenance training instead of taking a video course and hoping.
fieldNote: Her long horizon creates a **career stake**, not an assumed retirement escape.
Her union agenda covers **paid hours** and safe isolation; future maintenance vacancies and wages remain uncertain.

steps.text: Keep current press lead shifts while paid and safely guarded
Seek paid maintenance training terms through the union committee

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because the loader crew could lose paid hours quickly and a lead title may not save my night premium. A supervised paid trial, funded practical training and real local postings with clear wages would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I did not ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who signs the batch record when a robot loads the trays. The foil seam still has to hold after everyone goes home.

headlineQuote: The foil seam still has to hold after everyone goes home.
portrait: **Nora**, 27, leads a sterile packaging line after a two-year technical diploma and uses AI fault logs every day.
Her **higher operator pay**, partner, strong savings and many nearby factories give her room to search.
She wants **paid practical access** to new controls and brings staffing and safety questions to her union.
Fast robots threaten her **night premium**, while longer timelines allow a conditional route into maintenance.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could cut loading hours and Nora’s night premium before a comparable job is posted.
whatWouldHelp: A **paid supervised trial**, funded practical training and posted local jobs with clear wages would help.
